## Diagnosing Idle Stall on Renault Megane 2 (2005, 1.6L)

If your engine runs for ten seconds then dies, or requires keeping the pedal depressed to stay above 2000rpm, you are facing a classic low-RPM airflow starvation issue. The symptoms describedâstarting fine, stalling immediately after warm-up attempts, and recovering only when RPMs are manually held highâpoint directly to the Idle Control Valve (ICV) or its associated electrical circuit failing to maintain baseline air volume.

On the Renault Megane 2 with the 1.6L engine, the ICV is not a standalone component sitting loosely on the intake manifold like older mechanical systems. It is integrated into the throttle body assembly. This integration is a specific design choice by Renault that often trips up DIY mechanics looking for a "pop-off" valve to replace independently.

### Locating the Component

The IDLE CONTROL VALVE (ICV) is located inside the throttle housing, directly behind the butterfly plate. In your provided photos, you are looking at the top of the intake manifold where the throttle body sits. The ICV looks like a small cylindrical solenoid with two electrical connectors plugged into it. It does not have an external air hose connecting to it for vacuum actuation; instead, it is electrically controlled by the Engine Control Unit (ECU) to modulate the idle speed by opening or closing internal vanes.

To access it on this specific engine:
1.  Remove the air filter box and the intake ducting connected to the throttle body.
2.  Unplug the two electrical connectors attached to the ICV solenoid.
3.  You will likely need to unbolt the throttle body assembly from the intake manifold flange.

Once the throttle body is removed, the ICV becomes visible inside the housing. It is crucial to note that on many 1.6L K7M/K9K engines of this era, the ICV is often stuck open or closed due to carbon buildup or mechanical failure within the valve mechanism itself. Simply unplugging it and letting the engine run will not fix a mechanically jammed unit; the ECU might try to compensate by commanding higher RPMs, but if the physical vane cannot move, the airflow remains restricted at idle.

### Electrical Verification Before Replacement

Before ordering a new part, verify the electrical side of the failure. If the ECU is receiving valid input signals but the valve does not move, the issue could be a failed motor inside the solenoid or a wiring harness problem.

Use a multimeter to check for voltage at the ICV connectors while the ignition is on but the engine is off (or during a stall attempt if safe). The ECU typically provides a duty-cycle signal rather than constant DC power. If you see 0V or erratic readings, trace the wires back to the throttle body harness connector. A common pitfall in this specific vehicle is moisture ingress in the boot of the connector, causing intermittent connection loss that mimics a failed valve.

### The Throttle Body Integration Trade-off

A significant limitation when replacing the ICV on this platform is the integration with the throttle position sensor (TPS). On some variants, these are separate; on others, they share a common housing or calibration baseline. If you replace just the ICV without resetting the throttle body adaptation, the ECU may not correctly interpret the throttle plate angle relative to the new valve's zero point.

After installation, you will need to perform an idle adaptation procedure. This is usually done by disconnecting the battery negative terminal for 10â15 minutes to reset the learned fuel trims and idle values, or by using a diagnostic scanner to clear adaptation memory. Skipping this step often results in rough idling even with a brand-new ICV installed.

### Final Considerations

While changing spark plugs is a valid maintenance step, it rarely resolves airflow starvation at low RPMs unless the engine is already misfiring heavily. If the ICV is electrically dead or mechanically seized, replacing the entire throttle body assembly is often more cost-effective and reliable than attempting to source a standalone replacement valve, as finding an exact match for the internal solenoid can be difficult depending on the specific engine code (K7M vs K9K). Always inspect the rubber gasket on the back of the throttle body before reinstallation to ensure no air leaks are introduced at the manifold interface.
